source: Huang, Liu, He, Gilpin (2026) Learning to Draw ASCII Improves Spatial Reasoning in Language Models (Text2Space)
finding: Closest test of gaps 1 and 3. Models read a given ASCII grid well but draw one poorly from text. Drawing a grid before answering did not help, and drawing first dropped accuracy below the text-only baseline.
numbers: Table 2 answer accuracy, text only vs given ASCII vs both vs draw-then-answer (one turn): GPT-4.1 71.7 / 75.3 / 78.4 / 66.9 (own ASCII accuracy 41.7); GPT-OSS-20B 85.8 / 90.1 / 92.8 / 83.8 (ASCII acc 50.5); Qwen3-235B 93.3 / 92.7 / 97.0 / 91.9 (42.8); Qwen3-30B 84.8 / 89.0 / 90.1 / 82.3 (45.4). Generated ASCII accuracy only 12-50% across models. Answer-then-draw roughly equals text only.
quote: Models can reason over spatial layouts when provided, but cannot yet produce them reliably enough to support their own reasoning.
limits: Open and mid-size models plus GPT-4.1; no Claude or GPT-5. Directional-relation questions from text, not navigation. Tokens not matched, but the drawing adds tokens and does not pay for itself.
agent_relevance: A self-drawn grid only helps if it is right; when wrong it hurts. Do not add an unchecked draw step by default. Use a provided or verified grid.

source: Huang et al. (2026) Text2Space: consistency check and transfer results
finding: Gap 3: a cheap self-check exists. When the drawn ASCII agrees with the text answer, accuracy is high. Training on drawing transfers, but that is training, not scaffold.
numbers: Table 3 (draw first, one turn): Qwen3-235B answer accuracy 84.2, drawing and answer consistent in 67.8% of cases, accuracy on consistent cases 95.0. GPT-OSS-20B 94.3 / 75.9% / 97.0. Qwen3-30B 71.1 / 46.1% / 88.5. Table 4 zero-shot transfer for Qwen3-30B fine-tuned on drawing: StepGame +9.9, bAbI19 +17.0, SpartQA +43.3 points. Human check, 11 raters: description only 0.866, description plus ASCII 0.981 (+11.5).
limits: Consistency is a filter, not a fix, and costs a second generation. Fine-tuning result is out of scope for a scaffold-only agent (section 4b).
agent_relevance: Draw, then compare with the answer, gives a trust signal for one extra output. Use it as a trigger: if they disagree, re-derive.

source: Rodriguez Salgado Gonzalo (2026) From Pixels to BFS: High Maze Accuracy Does Not Imply Visual Planning (MazeBench)
finding: Frontier models, including Claude 4.6 and 4.7, solve image mazes by first turning the image into a text grid and then searching in prose. Giving the correct text grid instead of the image lifts Claude hugely and cuts tokens.
numbers: 110 mazes, 5x5 to 20x20, 19 model configs. GPT-5.5 96/100, GPT-5.4 91, Gemini 3.1 Pro 79. Table 5: Sonnet 4.6 image 6/100 at 14,313 tokens per solve vs text grid 80/100 at 3,222; Opus 4.7 image 31/100 at 13,189 vs text grid 90/100 at 2,285. Without reasoning budget all configs score 2-15%. On 20x20 ultra-hard mazes GPT-5.5 medium solves 4/10. A prompt forbidding grids and search was ignored by Sonnet 4.6; GPT-5.4 low scored 17/20 vs 19/20 standard.
limits: Grid was supplied by the experimenter, not drawn by the model, so it tests a correct text state, not self-drawing. One independent author, preprint. 100-maze core set.
agent_relevance: Strong support for a text-grid state as the working format and for a correct state beating perception (gaps 9, 10). The scaffold-only text-grid route reaches 90% on mazes up to 20x20 with enough reasoning tokens. The weak step is image-to-grid extraction.

source: Menon, Zemel, Vondrick (2024) Whiteboard-of-Thought: Thinking Step-by-Step Across Modalities
finding: Gaps 2 and 9: the model writes plotting code, the code renders an image, the model reads it. Drawing wins where text knowledge of the layout is poor (visual ASCII art, hexagons) and loses where text already handles the layout (square grids).
numbers: GPT-4o. Spatial navigation overall: Direct 33, CoT 42, WoT 52. Square grid: CoT 98 vs WoT 50 (Direct 68). Hexagon: CoT 8 vs WoT 61. Circle: CoT 25, WoT 41. ASCII word categories, CoT vs WoT: 3D 0 vs 92.1; Basic 0 vs 78.0; Dot Matrix 0 vs 11.8; Bubble 100 vs 42.1. WoT error analysis: 75% visual perception, 21% poor visualization, 4% code execution.
limits: GPT-4o only (2024). The image is perceived again by the model, so most failures are reading, not drawing. Tokens not matched.
agent_relevance: A router signal: if the layout has a standard text form the model knows (square grid, table), use text; if it is irregular or visual-only, a rendered or drawn state may help. Perceiving a rendered image is the main failure.

source: Hayashi, Hirata (2026) Limits of Spatial Imagery Reasoning in Frontier LLM Models
finding: Gap 5: a code tool that renders and rotates a 3D model did not close the rotation gap. A reset-to-canonical-view command turned the task into 2D matching.
numbers: SpatialViz 3D rotation. Human 79.16. Baselines: GPT-5.2 50.0; Claude-3.7-Sonnet 37.5; Claude-Opus-4.5 37.5; Gemini-3.5-Pro 37.5; Llama-4-Maverick 36.25; Grok-4.1 20.0 (table rows partly shifted in extraction). With tool and incremental rotation: 50-62.5% across 10 runs. 360-degree hint: 52.5% (one run). Reset enabled: 85-97.5%. GPT-5.4 45-52% (3 runs). Gemini-3-pro failed to finish in 12 hours. 97.5% and 62.5% imply about 40 test items (our inference).
limits: One task type, one main model (GPT-5.2), small item count. The model never confirmed a match by continuous rotation.
agent_relevance: The minimum useful tool is not a renderer. It is a tool that puts both objects in one canonical frame so the compare step is 2D. For rotation, ask for a canonical form or invariant, not a movie.

source: McCarty, Morales (2025-26) Artificial Phantasia: Evidence for Propositional Reasoning-Based Mental Imagery in LLMs
finding: Gap 4, re-opened. 60 imagine-and-name items (12 from Finke et al. 1989, 48 new). Reasoning models beat 100 online humans. Claude Opus 4.1 matched humans, not beat them. Image generation made the best OpenAI model worse.
numbers: Human mean 2.85/5 (SD 1.51), N=100, each saw 15 of 60 sets. o3 3.13 (U=110882, p=.0067); o3-Pro 3.31; GPT-5 3.35; Gemini 3 Pro 3.65 (p<.0001); o4-mini 2.66 (p=.441); Claude Opus 4.1 2.65 (p=.590); o3 with GPT-image-1 2.77. Bonferroni alpha .0028. GPT-5 by reasoning effort: high 3.35, medium 2.97, low 2.53, minimal 2.04. Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 2.0 Flash and open models did poorly. VVIQ correlated slightly negatively with human performance. Claude budgets: Sonnet 4 4000 thinking tokens, Opus 4.1 9000.
quote: The door for non-pictorial mental imagery has certainly reopened.
limits: Single group, one item family, online human sample. 12 of 60 items may be in training data (authors argue the 48 novel items rule this out). No independent replication found. Items are compositional shape assembly, doable with symbolic coordinates.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open for replication. Useful for the schema: more reasoning tokens raised the score (2.04 to 3.35) and an extra image channel lowered it. Supports text-first spatial thinking with enough reasoning budget.

source: Guo et al. (2026) Can LLMs See Without Pixels? SiT-Bench
finding: Gap 8, text side: text-only descriptions with coordinates let 2026 models reach 59% overall. Mental rotation, perspective shift and cognitive mapping stay hard. Thinking mode helps.
numbers: 3,800+ items, 17 subtasks. Human 74.42. Random 27.30. Gemini-3-Flash with thinking 59.46 (best). Qwen3-VL-32B 45.9 to 51.06 with thinking; Qwen3-8B 37.91 to 45.04. DeepSeek-V3.2 37.06. Cognitive mapping best model 8.34 vs human 26.44. Latency Gemini-3-Flash thinking 40.11 s. Specialized spatial models (Cosmos-Reason2-8B 42.13) lost to general Qwen3-VL-8B 45.66. Failure mode: arithmetic-spatial hallucinations.
limits: Text input only, no image arm, so it cannot give a text-vs-image gap number. No Claude in the headline rows I read.
agent_relevance: Text with coordinates is enough for local and relational questions. Global consistency and rotation need more than a longer description. Thinking budget is the cheapest lever.

source: Kancheti et al. (2026) Chain-of-Thought Degrades Visual Spatial Reasoning Capabilities of Multimodal LLMs
finding: Gaps 8 and 2: on perceived images, text CoT does not help spatial tasks. 7 of 8 reasoning models fail to beat their own backbone, and 6 of 8 do better with a plain direct-answer prompt than with their native CoT. GPT-5 and GPT-5-nano did slightly better without CoT.
numbers: 17 models, 13 spatial benchmarks. CoT lowers accuracy by about 3% on average across MLMs. Non-CoT minus CoT for GPT-5 +0.65 and GPT-5-nano +1.23; GPT-4o and GPT-4.1-mini gained under 0.5 from CoT. Native CoT vs non-CoT averages for reasoning models: ViGoRL 60.68 vs 62.52, TreeVGR 61.11 vs 62.60, R1-Ov 46.88 vs 47.84. Exception: GThinker CoT 62.52 vs non-CoT 39.38 (-23.14), caused by the model not following the direct-answer format. No-Image++ ablation: reasoning models pick wrong answers from text priors on a blank image.
limits: Perceived images, mostly open Qwen2.5-VL family. Not a model-drawn state test.
agent_relevance: With a perceived image, extra text reasoning can hurt. The same CoT can help once a text state exists. Format of the input decides whether thinking helps.

source: Sun et al. (2026) Reading, Not Thinking: The Modality Gap When Text Becomes Pixels in MLLMs
finding: Gaps 8 and 9, mechanism: same content as image vs text. The gap depends on font and resolution, and the main cause is that image input suppresses reasoning effort.
numbers: 7 MLLMs, 7 benchmarks, 5 input modes. GSM8K gaps exceed 60 points for several models. Font alone swings accuracy by up to 47 points. Image input gives 5-19x shorter outputs. Natural document images show much smaller gaps. Self-distillation on own text-mode traces closes the gap (over 50% improvement). GPT-5.2 example: MMLU text 92.33 vs pure image 91.06.
limits: Text rendered as pixels, not spatial scenes. The remedy is fine-tuning.
agent_relevance: Scaffold rule: when the input is an image, force the same step-by-step output as in text mode. Part of the gap is a prompt and rendering artifact, so 2024 gaps (IsoBench) may overstate current ones.

source: Tian et al. (2026) LAST: Leveraging Tools as Hints to Enhance Spatial Reasoning for MLLMs
finding: Gap 5, side evidence: perception tools (detection, depth, size estimation) returning annotated images and text hints lift closed models too, but not uniformly.
numbers: Gemini-2.5-Pro with tools: +18.00 on CVBench 2D relations, +14.90 on 3D distance. Gemini-3-Flash: -8.06 on 3D distance, over +12 on perception-dominant tasks. A 7B model trained with the tools: 55.35 to 73.64 average. Closed-model averages without tools: GPT-5.1 54.00, Gemini-2.5-Pro 57.80.
limits: Mostly a trained 7B system. Tools are perception tools, not rotation or drawing tools.
agent_relevance: Tools help where the model must measure something. A weaker model can be hurt on multi-step spatial inference. Not an answer to the minimum-tool question for rotation.

source: Jiang, Qin, Li (2026) SpatialText: A Pure-Text Cognitive Benchmark for Spatial Understanding in LLMs
finding: Gap 2: with text only, models retrieve stated facts and work in allocentric (global) coordinates well, but fail at egocentric perspective change and local reference frames.
numbers: Dual-source benchmark: human-annotated descriptions of real 3D indoor scenes plus code-generated scenes (12 questions per scene for epistemic tests). Headline accuracy values were not cleanly extracted, so none recorded.
limits: Abstract and method read; table values not recorded.
agent_relevance: Task feature that predicts trouble: a change of viewpoint or reference frame. A global coordinate list is fine. A frame change needs a recode step (convert to global coordinates first).

source: Lin et al. (2026) MentalThink: Shaping Thoughts in Mental SVG World
finding: Gaps 9 and 10, under training: with the same teacher and supervision, only the form of the thought differed. SVG thoughts beat text and boxes. The model also draws less on easy tasks.
numbers: Table 3 (MindCube / VSIBench): Think-with-Text 42.5 / 24.5, Think-with-BBox 41.1 / 17.4, Think-with-SVG 57.8 / 39.4. Final model 55.1% VSIBench, 76.0% MindCube. SVG data added 13.4 points average (31.0 to 44.4). Table 4: perception tasks 1.19 turns, 18.5% SVG calls, 109.2 tokens; compositional reasoning 1.64 turns, 63.7% SVG calls, 544.5 tokens; accuracy 55.11 vs 55.10.
limits: Fine-tuned (SFT plus RL), not scaffold-only. Tokens differ strongly between regimes and are not matched across paradigms.
agent_relevance: Nearest controlled same-model test of who makes the picture: a self-made executable drawing beats text when the model is trained to use it. Also shows a draw-or-not router that tracks task type.

source: Yang et al. (2026) How and What to Imagine? Visual Thinking in Unified Multimodal Models for Cross-View Spatial Reasoning
finding: Gap 9: with plain fine-tuning, the model's own generated thinking-image is nearly ignored. Dropping it at inference barely changes accuracy. A text CoT did worse than no thinking at all.
numbers: Text CoT scores across benchmarks in the appendix: 56.0, 60.4, 44.4, 40.8, 24.6, 25.3, 29.4, 35.8, 26.0, 54.9 (95% CIs given). Best visual variant gains over Text CoT: +7.3, +5.3, +3.4 on three benchmarks. Generate-then-blind probe across 4 out-of-domain benchmarks.
limits: Unified multimodal models trained on synthetic scenes. The fix (View Dropout) is training-time, not a scaffold.
agent_relevance: A drawn state can be decorative. Check that the answer actually uses it, for example by asking the agent to cite the cell it relied on.

source: LTD-Bench team (2025) LTD-Bench: Evaluating LLMs by Letting Them Draw
finding: Gap 3: drawing is the hard direction. Reasoning helps reading drawings but not producing them.
numbers: Only DeepSeek-R1 averages above 70%; GPT-4.1-mini above 60%; Qwen2.5-72B and Llama3.3-70B about 30%. R1 recognition average 71.54 vs V3 58.51. R1 beats GPT-4.1-mini by over 25 points in recognition but lags in generation. R1-distilled Llama3.3-70B: +18.05 on recognition, -2.91 on generation.
limits: Dot-matrix and code drawing tasks, 2025 models, no Claude in what I read.
agent_relevance: Matches Text2Space: reading a grid is easier than writing one. A drawn-state step needs a check because writing is the weak half.

source: Spagna, Hajhajate, Liu, Bartolomeo (2021) Visual mental imagery engages the left fusiform gyrus, but not the early visual cortex: a meta-analysis of neuroimaging evidence, Neurosci Biobehav Rev 122:201-217
finding: Gaps 6 and 7: an actual fMRI meta-analysis. Across 27 visual-imagery experiments there was no consistent early visual cortex activation, and a Bayesian test supported the null. This cuts against the V1 case for depictive imagery.
numbers: 46 experiments in 41 studies. 27 imagery-vs-control experiments (376 foci, 380 subjects); 4 imagery-vs-perception (62 foci, 52 subjects); 15 motor imagery (340 foci, 239 subjects). Left fusiform hotspot (Fusiform Imagery Node) plus fronto-parietal networks. Bayes factor under 0.33 in early visual areas. A 10-experiment imagery-vs-rest control also showed no early visual activity. Kilintari 2016 found a decrease in occipital BOLD.
limits: fMRI coordinates only: activation, not representation. Authors are fronto-parietal-network proponents, so a depictive-side rebuttal is worth checking; none found this session.
agent_relevance: The neural case for a picture format in V1 is not settled. Do not cite V1 as proof that images must be pictures.

source: Kosslyn, Thompson, Kim, Alpert (1995) Topographical representations of mental images in primary visual cortex, Nature 378:496-498
finding: Founding PET claim: imagery with eyes closed activates primary visual cortex. Image size relates to the location of peak activity, but only when the baseline is a non-imagery task with the same cues.
numbers: Abstract only: PET; imagery vs auditory-cue baseline showed V1 activation; a resting baseline hid the effect. N not in the abstract.
limits: Abstract-level. Baseline choice decided the result, which Spagna et al. (d15) treat as a weakness of this literature.
agent_relevance: Shows how fragile the founding neural evidence is to the control condition.

source: Kosslyn, Pascual-Leone, Felician et al. (1999) The role of area 17 in visual imagery: convergent evidence from PET and rTMS, Science 284:167-170
finding: rTMS over medial occipital cortex impaired the imagery task relative to sham, and also impaired the same task done by looking.
numbers: Abstract only: PET showed area 17 active while visualizing stripes; rTMS performance worse than sham. No N or effect size in the abstract.
limits: Spagna et al. (d15) argue rTMS over V1/V2 spreads to downstream areas, so it is not clean proof of V1 involvement.
agent_relevance: Strongest causal-style evidence for depictive imagery, with the spread caveat.

source: Chang, Zhang, Cao, Pearson, Meng (2025) Imageless imagery in aphantasia revealed by early visual cortex decoding, Curr Biol 35:591-599
finding: V1 carried decodable imagery content equally well in aphantasia and controls, but in aphantasia it was ipsilateral and did not cross-decode with perception.
numbers: Abstract only: decoding equal across groups; perceptual BOLD response lower in aphantasia. N not in the abstract.
limits: Abstract-level. Shows V1 content can exist without reported experience.
agent_relevance: Representation and experience can split. Supports judging the agent by function, not by whether it sees a picture.

source: Kosslyn, Ball, Reiser (1978) Visual images preserve metric spatial information, JEP:HPP 4:47-60; Intons-Peterson (1983) Imagery paradigms: how vulnerable are they to experimenters' expectations? JEP:HPP 9:394-412
finding: Gap 6: founding scanning result and the main demand-effect challenge, both at abstract level. Kosslyn 1978: scan time rises with distance across four experiments, larger images take longer, and without an instruction to use images distance had no effect. Intons-Peterson 1983: expectations moved results in all four experiments.
numbers: Kosslyn 1978: four experiments. Intons-Peterson 1983: four experiments (acuity, map scanning, rotated-hands priming, observer probe). Performance followed experimenters' beliefs in all of them. Observers named the beliefs correctly but could not say which cues differed. Shepard-Metzler 1971 abstract: RT linear in angular difference and no shorter for picture-plane than depth rotation. No slopes or Ns in any of the abstracts.
limits: Abstracts only. Exact slopes (Kosslyn r near .97), Ns, and Jolicoeur-Kosslyn 1985 reply numbers remain unconfirmed: the PubMed record for Jolicoeur-Kosslyn 1985 (Mem Cognit 13:320-332) has no abstract. Goldston et al. 1985 (subjects' expectations and scanning) also no abstract.
agent_relevance: Time patterns can be shaped by instructions, so a model that slows down proves nothing about format. Test accuracy, not latency.

source: Borst & Kosslyn (2008) scanning in imagery and perception; 2006 comparison of two image-scanning paradigms; 2016 children's scanning (abstracts via European PMC)
finding: Gap 6: scanning replicates, but its cause is mixed. Imagery slopes match perception slopes when the image comes from a just-seen pattern. Memory-based images scan more slowly. The Kosslyn and Finke-Pinker scanning tasks do not correlate, so scanning may be two processes.
numbers: Borst & Kosslyn 2008: scan time rose with distance at comparable rates in imagery, perception and iconic image (Exp 1); with long-term-memory images, scanning was slower, yet individual rates in perception and imagery correlated (Exp 2). 2006 study (3 experiments): same dot arrays, longer scan times in the Kosslyn paradigm, no consistent slope correlation between paradigms. 2016 study: N=282 children and adults; scanning effect present at 5 years, but misleading top-down distance cues changed scanning only from about age 8.
limits: Abstracts only; effect sizes not available; authors of the 2006 and 2016 papers not recorded.
agent_relevance: Even the classic result splits into at least two mechanisms (transforming the image vs shifting attention). A schema step called visualise should be split into named operations.

source: Meta-analyses of mental rotation: Voyer et al. (2011) time limits; 2023 infants; 2026 sex differences; Zacks (2008) neuroimaging (abstracts via European PMC)
finding: Gap 7: meta-analyses of mental rotation exist but concern sex differences and neural location, not the slope of RT on angle. None pools the Shepard-Metzler slope. Zacks (2008) says rotation activates intraparietal sulcus, supporting analog spatial representations, and motor areas under some conditions.
numbers: 2026: 41 studies, 59 effect sizes, men better, d = 0.60, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.67, Egger test no publication bias, high heterogeneity; the Mental Rotation Test gave the largest effect. 2023: 62 experiments, 1,705 infants aged 3-16 months, male infants slightly more reliable. Voyer 2011: 36 effect sizes, gender gap larger under time limits and linear in time available.
limits: Abstract-level. No pooled ms-per-degree value found. Search limited because OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were rate-limited.
agent_relevance: Rotation is a reliable graded human skill. The missing pooled slope means the human time-cost baseline still has no cited number.

source: MazeBench (2026) read for the image-versus-text gap trend, with SiT-Bench and Hayashi rotation numbers
finding: Gap 8: 2026 image-vs-text gaps for Claude are still very large on mazes. They are smaller for Opus 4.7 than Sonnet 4.6, but not closed. IsoBench numbers are from 2024 models on different tasks, so no like-for-like trend exists.
numbers: Maze: Sonnet 4.6 image 6% vs text grid 80% (74 points); Opus 4.7 image 31% vs text grid 90% (59 points). Older IsoBench gaps: 28.7 (Claude-3 Opus), 18.7 (GPT-4 Turbo), 14.9 (Gemini Pro). Rotation: Claude-Opus-4.5 37.5 vs human 79.16 (Hayashi table).
limits: Different tasks and difficulty. Only Claude and OpenAI numbers. No GPT-5 or Gemini 3 image-vs-text pair on IsoBench or SpatialEval was found.
agent_relevance: Keep a text-first state for any spatial task. Do not assume image input has caught up.
